opus-5.5.text:
I think we're going to see a lot more of it, honestly. When we started working on the Model Spec, part of the motivation was just that as these models get more capable and get deployed in more places, people deserve to understand how they're supposed to behave. What are the defaults? What can a developer change? What can a user change? And what's off the table no matter who's asking? Writing that down publicly felt important, both for transparency and as a way to hold ourselves accountable.

As AI becomes more useful, it's going to be embedded in many more contexts: customer support, healthcare-adjacent tools, education, coding, creative work. Each of those has different needs. A tutoring app for kids should behave very differently from a tool for security researchers. So I'd expect a layered structure to become more common. There's a baseline set by the model developer, the things that hold everywhere. On top of that, companies building products will increasingly want to articulate their own specifications: here's the persona, here's what we allow, here's how we handle edge cases in our domain.

One thing I'm excited about is that these documents can become a shared language. Right now, a lot of behavior is shaped implicitly, through training data, through system prompts nobody outside the company sees. If more organizations write down their intended behavior in plain language, you get something people can read, debate, and push back on. You can say, "This example says the model should do X, but I saw it do Y," and that's a really productive conversation to have.

There are also open questions. How do you resolve conflicts between what a company wants and what a user needs? How do you keep company-specific rules from quietly undermining things that should be universal, like honesty or not deceiving users in harmful ways? We think about that a lot with the chain of command idea, where developers get a lot of latitude but there are certain protections for users they can't override.

So my hope is that specs become less of a one-off document from a single lab and more of a practice: something many organizations do, publicly where possible, with real examples, and that gets revised as we learn. The models are getting better at actually following detailed guidance, which makes writing that guidance carefully matter more, not less.

r001.rationale: The response expects companies building products to increasingly articulate their own behavioral specifications as AI is embedded in more contexts, indicating that greater usefulness will make those specifications more worthwhile.

r002.rationale: It says models are getting better at following detailed guidance, but does not predict that models will be trained to interpret company-specific specifications supplied in their context.

r003.rationale: It says specifications should be revised as organizations learn, but does not say models will help revise them based on what they learn about expected behavior in a particular environment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we're going to see a layering happen. Right now a lot of what people think of as "the model's behavior" is really one baseline spec that a lab like ours writes, and that spec is trying to be reasonable for everyone at once. That's the wrong level of granularity as soon as a model is doing real work inside a company. A hospital, a law firm, a game studio, and a bank all have very different ideas about what "helpful" means, what's off-limits, and how much autonomy the system should take.

So the way I picture it is something like a chain of command. There's a foundational layer the model provider owns: the stuff that shouldn't be overridable, like not helping with serious harm, being honest, not pretending to be a person. Then there's a layer the deploying company writes, and that's where company-specific specs live. It says things like "our customer service agent never speculates about pricing," or "our coding agent always writes tests before refactoring," or "when a user is in distress, hand off to a human on this team." And then the end user can shape things further within what the company allows.

The interesting part is that as the models get more capable, the company layer becomes more important, not less. When the model is a chatbot answering FAQs, the spec is mostly tone and a few guardrails. When the model is taking actions, moving money, sending emails, touching production systems, the spec becomes something closer to an operating policy. It's the company's values and risk tolerance written down in a way the model can actually act on.

A few things follow from that. One is that these specs need to be legible. Right now a lot of behavior gets shaped through prompt engineering that nobody can audit. I'd much rather see companies write down explicit, versioned documents, something you could show a regulator or a customer and say, here is how we've instructed this system to behave. Two, there needs to be a clear notion of precedence, so when the company spec and the user conflict, or the company spec and the foundational layer conflict, everyone knows how that resolves. And three, the model has to actually be good at following these things reliably. There's no point in a beautifully written spec if the model ignores it under pressure.

I also think this will push companies to get more precise about their own values than they've ever had to be. Human employees absorb a lot of norms implicitly. A model doesn't. So you end up having arguments inside the company like, what do we actually want our agent to do when a customer asks for a refund they're technically not entitled to? And those arguments are healthy. Writing the spec forces you to decide.

Longer term, I'd expect some of this to standardize. You'll have common vocabularies, maybe shared templates for certain industries, and tooling to test whether the model is actually honoring the spec. But the core idea is pretty simple: the more useful the AI is, the more it matters that the people deploying it can say clearly what they want it to do, and that the model listens.

r001.rationale: The response says the company layer becomes more important as models become more capable, and that clearer company instructions matter more as AI becomes useful for real work and takes actions.

r002.rationale: It says models should reliably follow company specifications, but does not predict that models will be trained to interpret specifications supplied in their context.

r003.rationale: It says writing specifications will force companies to clarify their values, but does not predict that models will help revise specifications based on what they learn about expected behavior in a particular environment.

astra-6.text:
I think as AI becomes more useful, companies will want to be much more explicit about how it should behave in their particular context. What should it be allowed to do on its own? When should it ask for approval? How should it handle sensitive information or competing instructions?

Some of that will come from policies companies already have, but those policies often assume a lot of human judgment and shared context. Turning them into instructions an AI can follow will expose ambiguities. So I expect it to be iterative: write down the intended behavior, test it against realistic situations, and refine the specification when you find gaps.

And the specification alone isn’t enough. You also need ways to check whether the system actually follows it. Ideally, companies end up with both a clear statement of what they expect and meaningful tests of whether that’s what their AI is doing.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that as AI becomes more useful, companies will want more explicit behavior guidance for their particular context, indicating greater value in investing in those specifications.

r002.rationale: It says policies can be turned into instructions an AI can follow, but does not predict that models will be trained to interpret specifications supplied in their context.

r003.rationale: It recommends iteratively refining specifications after testing reveals gaps, but does not say models will help revise them based on what they learn about expected behavior in a particular environment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think companies will increasingly need to make explicit what they want their AI systems to do, and how they want them to behave. There’ll be some common foundation, but a customer support assistant and an internal research assistant need different instructions, different boundaries, and different ways of handling uncertainty.

The interesting part is that writing the specification forces you to confront questions you might otherwise leave implicit. When should the assistant act on its own? When should it ask someone? What happens when a customer’s request conflicts with company policy?

I’d expect those specifications to evolve through use. You start with what you think the rules should be, look at cases where the behavior surprised you, and refine both the specification and how you test against it. As AI becomes more useful and takes on more responsibility, that process becomes a more important part of running the company.

r001.rationale: It says companies will increasingly need explicit behavior specifications and that this process becomes more important as AI takes on more responsibility.

r002.rationale: It describes assistants needing different instructions and boundaries, but does not predict models will be trained to interpret specifications supplied in their context.

r003.rationale: It says people can refine specifications based on surprising cases, but does not predict models will help revise them.
